newsitem.title: USA: S&P raises Farmers' intercompany pool ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P raises Farmers' intercompany pool ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's today has raised its claims-paying ability ratings on Farmers Insurance Exchange Intercompany Pool and related entities (see list below*) to single-A'-plus from single-A'-minus.

Additionally, Standard & Poor's has raised its rating on Farmers Insurance Exchange's $400 million Rule 144A surplus notes to triple-B'-plus from triple-B'-minus and its corporate credit rating to single-A'-plus from single-A'-minus. The outlook is negative.
The ratings are based on the following major rating factors:

-- Strong market position. Through a strategic emphasis on expansion of its targeted product lines, mainly within the 29 states in which it operates, Farmers has risen to become the fourth largest U.S. property/casualty group in 1995.

-- Catastrophe Exposure. Over the past two years, Farmers has implemented several steps to mitigate its exposure to catastrophes in California, Texas, and the midwest. Along with the California Earthquake Authority, Farmers Insurance Exchange, on its own, has been a market leader in implementing policy form changes, raising rates dramatically, and purchasing significant reinsurance at a reasonable cost. These steps have reduced their gross exposure by almost two-thirds. In Texas and in the midwest, Farmers has taken similar steps and has also reduced its exposure in these regions.

-- Capitalization. A significant portion of surplus is derived from notes, accounting for 50% of policyholder surplus, however, 3/4 of those are owned by various affiliates, namely Farmers Group Inc. and various other B.A.T. Industries PLC affiliates. This concentration is not expected to change in the near future.

-- Operating Results. Operating performance rebounded in 1996, partly a result of less catastrophe losses, and partly as a result of improved underwriting. Year-end 1995 results, though still negative reflecting the lingering effects of the Northridge quake have improved to return on revenues of 5.0%, return on assets of 0.9%, and return on surplus of 4.2%. Projected results for year-end 1996 show a marked improvement with net income over $200 million. True profitability is distorted because of the cost-sharing arrangement between Farmers and Farmers Group Inc.

-- Reserves. Reserves are skewed, somewhat caused by the personal lines nature and the significant catastrophe losses in recent years. They are also distorted by certain reinsurance arrangements. However, Standard & Poor's believes that reserves, which has been a historic strength for the company, are adequate.

-- Lack of geographic diversification. Geographic dispersion is below average, as the five largest states provide 64% of premium. California alone accounts for 31%, down from 39% in 1991, and Texas accounts for 18%. Dispersion is expected to improve gradually as the company expands eastward and penetration improves in the Midwest, but Farmers' measured approach to growth in new states is expected to prevent dispersion from equaling the industry average any time soon.

Standard & Poor's expects results to continue to improve as Farmers begins to reap the rewards from its risk mitigation strategy. In addition, capitalization should slowly improve as the company begins to generate its own capital.
* Farmers Insurance Co. of Arizona, Farmers Insurance Co. of Columbus (OH), Farmers Insurance Co. of Idaho, Farmers Insurance Co. of Washington, and Mid- Century Insurance Co. of Texas.
